institutionName: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Full freedom of choice (EU universities require 2/3 of total ECTS to be within home-uni faculty), I wanted to take courses in mechanical engineering

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, HKUST is very well organised

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not much, mostly videos and Zoom meetings _before_ the exchange. Information was however always readily available either online, or in-person at UST.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: On-campus dormitories or HKUST Jockey Club Hall (off campus, but with HKUST buses running directly to/from uni). The dormitories are two-person (gender separated) rooms with one bathroom shared across two such rooms (both rooms of same gender). This applies for the newer halls 8 and 9 (I was in Hall 8), whereas older halls (don't know which exactly) will have a large bathroom and showers shared by the entire floor of the hall (rather than individual rooms).

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: No cooking facilities (unless you get your own electric pots, pans, air-fryers etc. etc.), but decent (and not too pricey) canteens on campus.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Air-conditioning is paid on a per-use (time-wise) basis, but is not _that_ expensive (approx 0.9HKD/h). If you aren't used to the hot (and humid) climate, it _will_ be necessary (fall term) from August til at least mid-october.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Upon arrival, I went to the dorms to register, and then (a few days later) had to go to pick up my student ID (which is necessary for dorm access, library access, printing, identification, etc. etc.) and that was that. If you miss the ID pickup date, you can still pick it up later at a different location, emails will be sent out about _EVERYTHING_.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Administration for international students was quick to reply if necessary, as well as plenty of information being available online. Furthermore, you will get tons of e-mails about all sorts of things, ranging from general events and talks, to mandatory things for exchange students as well as general information.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Register early, especially if you're registering for 1000-level courses, as a lot of these are "common core", meaning a lot of students will be taking them. You can (and it's a good idea to) register for too many courses (to get a good position on the wait-list) and later drop them if you don't want them, or don't get a wait-list position. Also, depending on the course and the professor, the prerequisites for the courses can be/are quite strictly enforced, be way of this.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Quite a few professors' English proficiency is _not very good_, often being limited to reading aloud from slides, making some lectures mostly useless. On the other hand, the academic material itself is very good and well-structured (usually).

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: First number denotes year, their bachelor's degrees are 4 years long (so a 4xxx course is still bachelor's level). Difficulty varies wildly, but the exams are generally quite difficult. Everything is curve-graded, so getting a passing mark is "easy" but getting a good grade (A- and above) is rather difficult.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: More memorisation, otherwise a similar pace, but with 5 courses at once instead of 2 (as at the Science Campus). I'd estimate a 30-60% greater workload to UCPH depending on courses taken.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ELEC1010 (electronic and information technology)(common core business students' course) - nonsense course with easy course material and a deceptively difficult midterm and exam compared to course material

MECH1910 (Foundations of mechanical and aerospace engineering) (common core engineering course) - mostly nonsense course, with decent material, but poor teaching/lectures, no midterm, exam was of appropriate difficulty compared to course material

MECH1907 (Introduction to mechanical and aerospace engineering) - difficult but _very good course_ and lecturer, will be renamed and moved to 2xxx after this semester, appropriately difficult exam compared to course material

MECH2310 (Thermodynamics) - difficult course, very good, but very strict/harsh professor, exam was quite difficult compared to course material

COMP3311 (Database management systems) - The contents and learning goals are good, but the slides, and the teaching itself is rather poor. Exam was of appropriate difficulty compared to course material

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
This is based on my own expecience as well as from conversations with local students as well as other exchange students (on other courses than myself):
Mechanical Engineering, Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, and Computer Science (and Computer Engineering) are (considered) very, very difficult and stressful, but are also in my opinion quite fulfilling. Generally speaking, if you have coursers with a lot of tutorials and labs, you will not a have a lot of free time left over, so be mindful of that. Generally speaking, stay away from common core courses (a lot of 10xx, 11xx, 12xx courses are common core - show up to a lecture during add/drop, and if there's more than 100 people there, it's common core for sure, otherwise ask).

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Air-conditioning was paid separately (other fees), but not too expensive

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Hong Kong does not have it's own production, so _EVERYTHING_ is imported. A lot of western products are hideously expensive, and vegetables and fruit aren't cheap either. Otherwise, eating out (e.g. canteens or smaller local or chain restaurants) is _very_ cheap relative to DK, but does add up in the long run. Hong Kong has 0% VAT (sales tax), and as such, it's a great place to shop for clothes, electronics and other non-consumables when compared with Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Incredibly well-established clubs and sporting facilities on campus

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Athletic activities: very easy-to-find and accurate descriptions on school website, lots of options for lots of different sports as well as an on-campus gym. 
Cultural activities: usually announced by e-mail, quite a few of them throughout the semester
Social activities: not that many, also announced by e-mail.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I personally played squash, and was met by a bunch of very nice people in charge of the squash club (as part of the HKUST Student Union [HKUSTSU])

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go for a walk around the city, both on the north as well as south side of the harbour. Lots of hiking trails available; a group of exchange students very quickly established a hiking group on Instragram, and went on hikes several times a week.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The on-campus culture is a bit different from the day-to-day city culture. The on-campus culture feels not dissimilar to UCPH, but it took a while to get used to interacting with people, services, restaurants etc. etc. in the city.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Though local students may seem (and are) rather shy, don't be afraid to say hi to whomever you happen to be sitting next to during the first few weeks in the lectures halls, and see if you can strike up a conversation. Once you get to talking, they are usually very quick to open up, and quite happy to speak with you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
None in particular - if you don't already know, at least to some degree how to use chopsticks, do spend a bit of time practicing from home, it will help a great deal, as quite a few restaurants don't provide western cutlery by default (although I assume you can always ask for it). 
A lot of people (especially older than, say, 30) do not speak English very well, and you can forget all about pronouncing Cantonese words correctly (even simple phrases will easily go misunderstood or be met with a look of confusion) if you haven't practiced with someone local first.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are incredibly friendly and helpful (especially to foreigners), and are from my experience, quite eager to learn about Western culture, and a lot of them are quite interested in Denmark, specifically (happiest country and all that). Other than that, I was a great fan of the very down-to-earth way of socialising, e.g. grabbing lunch or dinner together, or having a relaxed drink at the on-campus Uni-bar, or simply going for a walk around campus.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
No preparation period/study break (læsuge) before/during midterm exams; life simply goes on, and you might easily have both a midterm exam and other lectures during the same day - can become very busy/hectic, so be prepared!

Get an Octopus Card (their Rejsekort) at the airport and top it up, other than there, it can only be topped up with cash (at 7-Eleven). Check your bank for international fees (e.g. I had 1.5% on every transaction and 3% on withdrawals), and get e.g. a Revolut account if the fees are high. 

Thoroughly explore your options during the add-drop period, so you get as many courses you actually want as possible. When requesting a prerequisite waiver (based on courses taken at your home institution), it might take a day or three to get the application processed, so things might not work out last-minute. If in doubt of anything, you can always, always, write the professor an e-mail, most are quick to respond.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Mingle with the locals, most are a bit shy but generally very sweet (and scarily smart)!

Some courses (depends on the lecturer) take attendance, which _usually_ counts towards your final grade (5-10%)

If you want to have time to go to the city during weekdays, make sure to plan your courses such that your day ends early, or beings _very late_ (e.g. only one lecture at 17 or 18), since getting to the city centre (or back to UST) takes ~1 hour.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Most definitely the number of new people whom I now consider friends, or even close friends, after just 4 months of stay. This is both local as well as other exchange students (I also met my now girlfriend [local] there, but I assume this is a slightly rarer occurrence ;))

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Definitely the balance of academics and free time. Admittedly, I did have a very busy schedule, even by UST standards (confirmed by local students) for only taking 15 credits (30ECTS), but generally speaking, UST is not a particularly relaxing place (neither is the entirety of Hong Kong, in my opinion), but it is very rewarding.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
